title: Two Coworkers Debate Letting AI Write Their Reports
script: Bima: [curious] Citra, have you tried letting the new AI tool draft our monthly reports? It cut my writing time in half yesterday.
Citra: [hesitant] I've tried it once, but honestly, something about it makes me uneasy, even though I can't fully explain why yet.
Bima: [reasonable] What exactly bothers you about it? The reports it produced looked fairly accurate to me, as far as I could tell.
Citra: [thoughtful] They were accurate on the surface, but the analysis felt generic, as if it could describe almost any team's month rather than ours specifically.
Bima: [considering] That's a fair point, although I edited mine afterward, so the final version still reflected our actual numbers and decisions.
Citra: [concerned] Even so, if we rely on it every month, won't we eventually lose the habit of noticing patterns ourselves, before the software notices them for us?
Bima: [thoughtful] I hadn't considered that. In spite of saving time now, we might be trading away a skill we'll need later.
Citra: [reasoning] Exactly my worry. Despite how convenient it feels, I'd rather write a rough draft myself first, then use the tool only to polish the language.
Bima: [curious] So you're not against using it entirely, just against depending on it for the actual thinking part?
Citra: [confirming] Precisely. As a result, I still understand what I'm reporting, instead of just approving whatever sentences appear on the screen.
Bima: [reflective] That approach seems reasonable, actually. Maybe the mistake isn't using the tool, but skipping the thinking step entirely because it's faster.
Citra: [warmly] Right, and if something in the report is ever questioned by management, I want to genuinely understand every sentence I submitted.
Bima: [determined] Fair enough. I'll write my own outline first from now on, then let the tool help with phrasing, the same way you do.
Citra: [smiling] That sounds like a healthier balance than what either of us was doing before this conversation, honestly.
Bima: [warmly] Agreed. Thanks for pushing back on this. I hadn't really questioned it until you brought up losing the habit of noticing patterns.
Citra: [kindly] That's what coworkers are for, I suppose. Questioning each other before a shortcut quietly becomes a permanent weakness.
